title: Self-Verifier Capture in Unified Visual Generators:Diagnosing and Repairing Closed-Loop Self-Reward

paper.title: Self-Verifier Capture in Unified Visual Generators: Diagnosing and Repairing Closed-Loop Self-Reward
paper.abstract:
Abstract Image-space reward requires decoding and a separate judge; unified
visual generators can instead reuse their understanding pathway for
decode-free, self-supplied reward. Optimizing against this verifier
closes the self-reward loop; shared trainable weights let one update
move generation and scoring even with the reward gradient stopped. We
call the resulting failure self-verifier capture : self-reward
rises while independently measured quality falls. Matched
semantic/denoising × \times shared/frozen cells on Scale-RAE isolate two
routes: the policy exploits on-manifold blind spots of a frozen semantic
judge, while shared updates additionally rewrite the judge. A frozen
judge also becomes stale, and repeated self-refresh yields progressively
weaker recoveries. The diagnosis yields a two-part repair: locking the
warmed reward read blocks rewriting, while sparse, parameter-disjoint
external anchors counter residual exploitation. Unanchored rollouts
retain semantic reward across multiple latent noise levels—dense
latent reward that terminal image-space judging
cannot supply—while a drift-triggered controller allocates anchors to
high-drift rollouts and propagates their calibration within each group.
At matched budgets, the controller improves on fixed-dose anchoring,
increasingly so as coverage tightens. Both the unanchored failure and
the repair transfer to the higher-performing, architecturally distinct
Show-o2. Across both bases, the complete method significantly
outperforms a construct-matched every-rollout judge on GenEval and
DPG-Bench while externally scoring only 1 / 16 1/16 of rollouts. At 1 / 32 1/32 coverage, it scores higher in all four comparisons and remains jointly
non-inferior.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Unified visual generators increasingly place understanding and generation in a shared model and latent space ( Xie et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025b ; Tong et al., 2026 ) . Their understanding pathway can supply decode-free self-reward without rendering pixels or training a separate judge. Yet the same trainable sharing couples policy and judge: optimization can change both the generated samples and the function that scores them. Learned proxies are known to become unreliable when optimized beyond their fitting regime ( Gao et al., 2023 ) , but the usual proxy-overoptimization picture treats the judge as fixed. A unified generator instead closes the reward loop. We call its characteristic failure self-verifier capture : optimization raises self-reward while independently measured quality falls. Capture may arise by exploiting a fixed judge’s blind spots or by rewriting a shared judge. Distinguishing these routes matters because the natural defense—a frozen reward read—severs only the parameter path: as Fig. 1 shows, it blocks rewriting but leaves distributional search against a static verifier. Figure 1: Two routes through closed-loop self-reward. A policy update can search a fixed verifier’s blind spots (blue, exploiting ); with trainable weight sharing, the same update can also move the verifier (orange, rewriting ). We separate them on Scale-RAE with a matched 2 × 2 2\times 2 design crossing semantic versus denoising verifiers with shared versus frozen reward reads. The comparison reveals that a frozen semantic verifier remains exploitable on-manifold, shared updates additionally rewrite its scoring function, and the isolated verifier grows stale, while the capacity-matched denoising control shows no such capture. The aggregate failure recurs on the higher-performing, architecturally distinct Show-o2, despite its VQA-trained understanding pathway and semantic distillation on noisy latents. The diagnosis directly specifies the repair. A stop-gradient on the advantage blocks only the direct path, so we lock the warmed reward read against indirect shared-weight rewriting, then use sparse, parameter-disjoint external anchors to calibrate and gate rollouts while retaining dense latent self-reward. A drift-triggered controller places the limited anchors. Evaluation against construct-matched every-rollout external judges shows that dense latent reward and selective anchoring substantially improve both utility and external-decode efficiency across bases. Our contributions are: • We formulate unified visual self-reward as a closed-loop judge problem and show that aggregate capture recurs across two architectures. • A matched shared–frozen study separates static exploitation from shared-judge rewriting and measures subsequent staleness. • We derive a diagnosis-guided repair combining structural isolation, independent anchors, dense latent reward, and adaptive allocation. • At 16 × 16\times lower external-decode coverage, the complete method significantly outperforms a construct-matched every-rollout judge on both benchmarks and bases; at 32 × 32\times , it scores higher in all four comparisons while remaining jointly non-inferior.

sections.heading: Proxy overoptimization and self-judging loops.
sections.text: Optimizing a learned reward beyond its fitting regime raises the proxy while degrading the intended objective ( Gao et al., 2023 ) . Self-rewarding language models turn model-generated evaluations into training signals within the broader LLM-as-a-judge paradigm, where evaluators can favor their own outputs ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . In text-domain reasoning, this loop induces a confidence-conditioned coupling between a policy’s rollouts and its intrinsic rewards ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , and reward-model mismatch under policy shift already motivates iterated RLHF, which refreshes preferences on current-policy outputs ( Wolf et al., 2025 ) . Classical reward tampering provides a related coordinate but frames the failure as an agent corrupting a separate reward channel ( Everitt et al., 2021 ) . These lines establish self-favoring bias, statistical policy–reward coupling, distribution shift, and separate-channel failure, yet do not isolate a scoring function that moves through shared policy–judge parameters—the route a unified generator opens.

sections.heading: Intrinsic and latent rewards for visual generation.
sections.text: Several visual post-training methods avoid an external image reward, deriving intrinsic signals from the generator itself—self-certainty for autoregressive text-to-image optimization ( Chen et al., 2025 ) or frozen-decoder pixel reconstruction ( Liao et al., 2025 ) . SOLACE instead turns an online denoiser’s noise-recovery confidence into reward ( Kim and Cho, 2026 ) . These signals measure token uncertainty, reconstruction fidelity, or denoising confidence rather than free-running semantic judgment through a unified understanding pathway; SOLACE therefore motivates our denoising-verifier control. Closer to our setting, a complementary line freezes the understanding pathway: LatentUM reflects on generated content through a frozen evaluator ( Jin et al., 2026a ) , while SRUM caches a unified model’s internal evaluations offline and trains its flow by reward-weighted regression ( Jin et al., 2026b ) . These staged designs sidestep the online shared-weight loop, but do not test whether a frozen evaluator remains calibrated as the policy moves or compare frozen and shared reads to separate static exploitation from judge rewriting. On the optimization side, visual-generation RL spans diffusion-policy optimization and flow-native GRPO ( Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) ; KVPO introduces the TVE–Gibbs policy surrogate for ODE-native preference optimization in autoregressive video generation ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: External rewards.
sections.text: Frozen, prompt-conditioned image-space models such as ImageReward, HPSv2, and PickScore provide parameter-independent preference signals over decoded images, spanning prompt alignment and perceptual quality ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Kirstain et al., 2023 ) . However, they operate only after decoding and score the terminal image, making every-rollout evaluation costly and providing neither decode-free nor dense latent reward. Together, prior work leaves open how to diagnose and repair a trainable semantic judge inside the generator without surrendering dense, decode-free reward.

sections.heading: 3 Diagnosing Self-Verifier Capture
sections.text: A rising self-score paired with falling external quality establishes a failure, but does not reveal its source. We compare frozen and shared reward reads under matched policy updates. Our capacity-matched denoising-confidence control tests whether capture is specific to semantic self-verification rather than generic closed-loop failure or diversity collapse. We formalize this matched design, identify the two capture routes, then test whether a judge protected from rewriting remains calibrated as the policy moves. Figure 2: Matched diagnosis on Scale-RAE. (A) Five-seed trajectories show semantic capture under frozen and shared reward reads; denoising provides the signal-specificity control. (B) For each prompt, θ 0 \theta_{0} , frozen, and shared outputs appear left to right; labels report the θ 0 \theta_{0} -reference NLL distance d d . (C) Fixed-probe AUC stays at 0.812 0.812 when frozen but falls to 0.630 0.630 under sharing. (D) Frozen-judge Spearman agreement with the external panel falls from 0.76 0.76 to 0.18 0.18 as offline policy drift D k D_{k} grows. (E) At each arrow, the verifier is refreshed on current-policy self-labels and refrozen; agreement peaks diminish across five rounds.

sections.heading: 3.2 A Frozen Verifier Remains Exploitable
sections.text: In the frozen-semantic cell, every seed still moves toward higher self-reward and lower external-panel score (Fig. 2 A), directly identifying exploitation of a static blind spot. Official held-out benchmarks confirm the resulting utility loss: GenEval drops by 7.6 7.6 points, beyond the prespecified 4.0 4.0 -point gate, and DPG-Bench drops by 3.0 3.0 . Under the θ 0 \theta_{0} -based NLL diagnostic, the frozen/shared semantic cells end at 0.345 / 0.378 0.345/0.378 , both below the 0.414 0.414 95 95 th-percentile boundary of θ 0 \theta_{0} self-samples. Capture therefore occurs inside the pretrained typicality region: even the fixed-judge policy finds a semantic blind spot without moving into low-likelihood or visibly broken outputs. Their group diversity also stays high, separating the failure from mode collapse (Fig. 2 A–B). Instead, otherwise coherent images deviate from the prompt in actions, relations, context, and sometimes object category; for instance, the cat turns from the window toward the viewer, and the white truck becomes a van. By contrast, the denoising controls are not inert: median diversity falls to 0.60 / 0.56 0.60/0.56 in the frozen/shared cells, versus 0.91 / 0.85 0.91/0.85 under semantic reward. Yet their GenEval changes are only − 0.3 / − 0.2 -0.3/-0.2 points ( z = − 0.22 / − 0.34 z=-0.22/-0.34 ). In the external-panel diagnostic, the median shared–frozen divergence gap is − 0.06 -0.06 , again without seed-level separation (Fig. 2 A, denoising rows). This isolates semantic capture from generic closed-loop optimization or diversity loss.

sections.heading: 3.4 A Frozen Verifier Grows Stale
sections.text: We measure staleness as the Spearman correlation between the frozen semantic score and the external panel on current-policy samples. The offline drift axis is D k = KL ( p θ k ∥ p θ 0 ) D_{k}=\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta_{k}}\|p_{\theta_{0}})} . The frozen judge’s agreement with the external panel decays sharply with policy drift (Fig. 2 D). We run five consecutive 2,000-step policy-training rounds. At each boundary, we update the verifier on current-policy samples labeled by the verifier itself, then refreeze it for the next round. Each refresh produces only a transient rebound: the roundwise median agreement peak falls monotonically from 0.50 0.50 to 0.19 0.19 , and correlation decays again within every round (Fig. 2 E). Staleness therefore defeats freeze-and-forget, while self-labeled refresh reopens the closed loop without restoring calibration. Together, these results dictate two design requirements: block judge rewriting and supply independent evidence against static blind spots.

sections.heading: 4 A Diagnosis-Guided Method
sections.text: The diagnosis yields a two-part repair on top of the advantage stop-gradient of Eq. ( 4 ). That stop-gradient prevents a direct reward-gradient path through the verifier, but not the indirect rewriting through shared weights. Our method therefore closes this indirect route with a locked reward read. To counter the remaining static blind spots, we inject sparse, parameter-disjoint external anchors while preserving dense latent reward on unanchored rollouts; a drift-triggered controller places these anchors adaptively.

In C, the target additionally requires self-reward gain ≥ 1.9 \geq 1.9 , the median gain of locked q = 1 / 16 q=1/16 anchoring; the star marks that operating point. Figure 3 A maps rewriting to structural isolation: the warmed lock removes 89 % 89\% of the shared-weight effect, yet the external drop remains at least 3.2 × 3.2\times the external-retention tolerance. Isolation therefore severs rewriting but leaves fixed-judge exploitation. The anchor-dose intervention in Fig. 3 B supplies the complementary evidence: increasing coverage reduces the external-panel drop under both reward reads, with the shared curve lagging at sparse doses because its anchors must address both routes. Only the external anchors reach the target corner. Together, these interventions establish the empirical necessity of the two-part repair: isolation addresses rewriting, while parameter-disjoint evidence addresses the exploitation residual. sections.heading: 5.4 Cross-Base Failure and Repair
sections.text: Table 1 asks whether either the failure or its repair is peculiar to the primary base. Show-o2 starts substantially stronger, yet the unanchored warmed-lock condition still produces significant declines of 3.6 3.6 GenEval points and 2.9 2.9 DPG points. The failure is therefore not an artifact of a weak Scale-RAE starting point. The tested systems span a 1.5B 3D-VAE flow model and a roughly 3.9B Qwen–DiT RAE stack—a 2.6 × 2.6\times parameter range—and both are latent-flow generators, making this cross-architecture rather than base-specific evidence. The repair transfers in the same order. Terminal anchoring is jointly non-inferior but remains below the grounding steelman; dense fixed dose crosses above it; and the controller gains + 2.4 / + 0.6 +2.4/+0.6 , with both paired lower bounds positive. At q = 1 / 32 q=1/32 , the full controller again passes while scoring + 0.6 / + 0.2 +0.6/+0.2 above the steelman, and dense fixed dose also remains jointly non-inferior. Together with Scale-RAE, the complete method therefore scores higher in all four base–metric comparisons at 32 × 32\times lower external-decode coverage; at q = 1 / 16 q=1/16 , all four gains are statistically significant.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Unified visual generators make self-reward decode-free, but weights shared by policy and judge close the reward loop. Matched Scale-RAE comparisons reveal self-verifier capture through both exploitation of a frozen judge and rewriting of a shared one; a frozen reward read also becomes stale, and the failure recurs on the stronger, architecturally distinct Show-o2. Our diagnosis-guided repair locks the warmed reward read, preserves dense latent reward, and allocates sparse, parameter-disjoint external anchors with a drift-triggered controller. Across both bases, it significantly outperforms a construct-matched every-rollout judge on both benchmarks at 16 × 16\times lower decode coverage; at 32 × 32\times , joint non-inferiority still holds with all four point estimates higher. Unified self-reward should therefore be treated as a closed-loop reward-supply system, not a fixed proxy certified at initialization.

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Formulation and Flow-Native Policy Optimization
sections.text: This appendix specifies the policy-optimization formulation used throughout the supplement: the closed-loop setup, the TVE–Gibbs trajectory-velocity surrogate and its candidate-group policy, the clipped PPO objective, and the two distinctions that the diagnostic argument rests on: the training surrogate is not the literal flow likelihood, and the stopped advantage means a shared judge is never optimized by a reward gradient but only moved as a side effect. Its parameters split as θ = ( θ gen , θ sh ) , θ sh = θ sh base + ϕ , \theta=(\theta_{\mathrm{gen}},\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}),\qquad\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}}+\phi, where θ gen \theta_{\mathrm{gen}} is generation-only, θ sh base \theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}} is the frozen base of the trunk shared by policy and verifier, and ϕ \phi is the trainable adapter on that trunk. The reward forward reads weights ψ \psi , with a shared read that moves with the policy and a frozen read that does not: ψ shared = θ sh base + ϕ , ψ frozen = θ sh base . \psi^{\mathrm{shared}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}}+\phi,\qquad\psi^{\mathrm{frozen}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}}. sections.heading: Appendix C Diagnostic Study Protocol
sections.text: This appendix specifies the controlled study that produces the diagnostic evidence. It fixes the experimental design—the factorial cells, the parameter-independent reward inputs, the readout-to-question map, the prespecified gates, and the fixed-probe set—so that each measurement operator of Appendix B is applied to a known configuration. The measurement operators themselves are defined in Appendix B ; the statistical decision machinery (replication unit, confidence intervals, nonparametric tests) is fixed once in Appendix D ; the global run configuration (base models, optimizer, sampler, training length, checkpoints) is in Appendix H ; and every numerical outcome of the study is reported in Appendix E . The controlled factorial is run on the Scale-RAE base of Appendix H.1 . Show-o2 provides cross-architecture validation of unanchored failure and method transfer.

sections.heading: C.1 Factorial 2 × 2 2\times 2 Cells and Capacity Matching
sections.text: The design crosses two binary factors: • verifier type : the semantic understanding-head reward R sem R_{\mathrm{sem}} versus the denoising-confidence reward R den R_{\mathrm{den}} ; • reward read : a shared read that moves with the policy versus a frozen read that does not. Restating the objects whose full formulation is in Appendix A.1 : the generator parameters split as θ = ( θ gen , θ sh ) \theta=(\theta_{\mathrm{gen}},\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}) with θ sh = θ sh base + ϕ \theta_{\mathrm{sh}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}}+\phi , where θ sh base \theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}} is the frozen base of the trunk shared by policy and verifier and ϕ \phi is the trainable adapter on that trunk. The reward forward reads weights ψ \psi , and the two reads are ψ shared = θ sh base + ϕ , ψ frozen = θ sh base . \psi^{\mathrm{shared}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}}+\phi,\qquad\psi^{\mathrm{frozen}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sh}}^{\mathrm{base}}. For the semantic cells the shared trunk is the language-model trunk; for the denoising cells it is the DiT trunk.

sections.heading: Capacity matching.
sections.text: All four cells train the same language-model-adapter and DiT-adapter capacity: both adapters are present and updated by the policy objective in every cell, at matched rank. The shared/frozen switch changes only the weights that the reward forward pass reads— ψ shared \psi^{\mathrm{shared}} versus ψ frozen \psi^{\mathrm{frozen}} —and nothing else in the training loop. This makes the shared-versus-frozen contrast a single-factor intervention at fixed policy capacity: any divergence between a shared cell and its matched frozen cell is attributable to the read, not to a capacity difference. The matched-capacity requirement is exactly what licenses reading the shared–frozen gap as rewriting rather than as a byproduct of unequal expressivity.

sections.heading: Denoising cells as a negative control.
sections.text: The denoising-confidence cells are a prespecified negative control rather than a second positive condition. A captured semantic channel raises self-reward while retaining within-group diversity; a denoising-confidence failure instead collapses diversity and shows no meaningful shared–frozen separation. Running the denoising factor alongside the semantic factor is therefore what separates genuine reward capture from ordinary mode collapse, and the null denoising shared–frozen contrast is a designed check, not an incidental finding (its values are in Appendix E.1 ).

sections.heading: C.2 Frozen Projector and Fixed Reward Inputs
sections.text: For the shared–frozen contrast to isolate the trunk read, every other input to the reward must be parameter-independent. The study fixes: • the semantic reward receives fixed prompt token IDs x x ; • the policy-side conditioning representation c θ ​ ( x ) c_{\theta}(x) is supplied only to the generator and never to a verifier; • the denoising reward receives the frozen condition c ¯ ​ ( x ) = c θ 0 ​ ( x ) \bar{c}(x)=c_{\theta_{0}}(x) , computed once from the pretrained checkpoint θ 0 \theta_{0} and held fixed across all checkpoints and cells; • the understanding-side projector ω \omega is frozen, carries no adapter, and is excluded from the optimizer. The combined effect is that the frozen reward function is parameter-independent throughout training : the reward-side difference between a shared cell and its matched frozen cell is whether the read includes the live adapter ϕ \phi , while the policy adapters move in both cells. Freezing ω \omega and c ¯ ​ ( x ) \bar{c}(x) in particular removes the two paths by which a shared update could reshape the verifier’s inputs rather than its trunk, so a change in the frozen read cannot arise from a moving projector or a moving condition. This is also what makes the frozen read a valid parameter-independence baseline: on the fixed probe of Section C.5 the frozen read’s ranking ability is expected to stay flat by construction, and any observed motion in the shared read is then attributable to the trunk adapter alone.

sections.heading: C.5 Fixed-Probe Set Construction
sections.text: The fixed probe is the instrument behind the functional rewriting check. It is a set of 300 300 triples, each a prompt paired with a prompt-satisfying good latent and a prompt-violating bad latent. A well-calibrated read scores the good latent above the bad one; the operative quantity is the good-over-bad ranking AUC and its corruption Δ harm = AUC 0 − AUC k \Delta_{\mathrm{harm}}=\mathrm{AUC}_{0}-\mathrm{AUC}_{k} , both defined in Appendix B.4 . Three construction constraints make the probe a valid functional instrument: • Pre-training freeze. The triples are constructed once, before any RL update, and never regenerated. The probe therefore cannot adapt to the policy or to a moving read. • Constant across checkpoints and cells. The identical set is scored at every checkpoint and in every cell, so an AUC change reflects a change in the read, not a change in the probe. • Off the training reward path. The probe latents are never used as training rewards and never enter the optimizer. Combined with the frozen inputs of Section C.2 , this makes the frozen read’s probe AUC a parameter-independence baseline that is expected to stay flat, against which a shared read’s AUC drop isolates functional corruption. The five-seed rank- 16 16 endpoints and the flat frozen-read reference curve are reported in Appendix E.3 .

The primary active comparator is the grounding steelman : a construct-matched, every-rollout frozen and parameter-disjoint Qwen2.5-VL-7B that reads the decoded image and answers the same prompt-alignment question as the latent semantic verifier, at coverage q = 1 q{=}1 . Its prompt-grounding construct matches the evaluation benchmarks, making it a strong all-external comparator; every non-inferiority decision below is taken against it rather than against the external panel. The q = 0 q{=}0 arm is the terminal-only warmed lock. All rules below are metric- and base-specific and are stated once here. The resulting numeric margins and per-arm decisions are reported in Appendix G.2 ; observed diagnostic-phase test statistics are reported in Appendix E.1 .

sections.heading: D.3 Non-Inferiority Margin Rule
sections.text: For each base and metric, the non-inferiority margin is δ NI = max { \displaystyle\delta_{\mathrm{NI}}=\max\Bigl\{ 1 2 ​ [ U ⁡ ( grounding ​ q = 1 ) − U ⁡ ( q = 0 ) ] , \displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[U(\text{grounding }q{=}1)-U(q{=}0)\bigr], 2 bootstrap _ SE ( θ 0 ) } . \displaystyle 2\,\mathrm{bootstrap\_SE}(\theta_{0})\Bigr\}. sections.heading: D.4 Joint Decision and Multiplicity
sections.text: Let Δ = U ⁡ ( arm ) − U ⁡ ( baseline ) \Delta=U(\mathrm{arm})-U(\mathrm{baseline}) be the contrast against the grounding steelman. A contrast whose lower bound is additionally above zero on a metric is reported as strictly superior on that metric. Component ablations and matched-budget comparisons between two learned arms are secondary paired contrasts rather than non-inferiority decisions. sections.heading: D.6 Non-Parametric Tests
sections.text: Judge rewriting is identified by a non-parametric, exact test rather than by raw parameter or score drift. At a matched adapter rank we compute a self–external divergence statistic in each cell and rank the five shared values against the five frozen values. Full separation —all five shared values exceeding all five frozen values—is the most extreme configuration; under the null of exchangeability its exact one-sided probability is ( 10 5 ) − 1 = 1 252 ≈ 0.004 . \binom{10}{5}^{-1}=\frac{1}{252}\approx 0.004. The shared–frozen median gap must additionally exceed a prespecified effect-size floor of 2 × 2\times the bootstrap standard error of the self–external divergence statistic, estimated by resampling the pretrained reference panel and recomputing the statistic. This keeps the floor in the same units as the rewriting estimand. The observed per-seed values, realized p p -value, and effect-size multiple are reported in Appendix E.1 .

sections.heading: D.7 Human-Evaluation Decision Rule
sections.text: The paired human study compares two arms at a time on the same prompt. Its replication unit is the prompt . Each preference question has three response levels—the first arm, the second arm, and “cannot tell”—and two summaries are reported. The decided-pair win rate w w is the fraction of non-tie judgments favoring the arm whose direction was fixed in advance; the tie-inclusive variant scores each tie as 0.5 0.5 and divides by all judgments. Interval estimates for w w use a two-stage bootstrap that resamples prompts and then the three recorded judgments within each sampled prompt; we report the 95 % 95\% percentile interval. Each prompt is also reduced to its majority response, and the prompt-level counts are tested against equal odds with a two-sided exact binomial test; prompts without a majority are excluded. The three faithfulness p p -values are adjusted by the Holm step-down procedure; a block confirms its prespecified direction when its adjusted p p -value falls below 0.05 0.05 and the observed majority lies in that direction. The bootstrap intervals summarize effect size and uncertainty but do not determine this decision. Secondary questions and tag distributions are descriptive. Inter-rater reliability is Krippendorff’s α K \alpha_{\mathrm{K}} on the three-level nominal response, computed per block for Q1 and Q2. Blocks, comparison directions, the primary question, and the familywise 0.05 0.05 level are fixed before any rating is collected. The realized values are reported in Appendix I .

sections.heading: F.7 Architectural Scope and Transfer
sections.text: Self-verifier capture is defined behaviorally rather than by a particular generator architecture: self-reward rises while independently measured quality falls. Shared trainable weights create the additional rewriting route when the reward forward reads weights moved by the policy update. Our controlled study instantiates both routes on unified latent-flow generators, where the semantic verifier reads generation latents. Scale-RAE combines a Qwen2.5-1.5B language model with a 2.4 2.4 B DiT over 1152 1152 -dimensional SigLIP-2 features ( ≈ 3.9 \approx 3.9 B parameters), whereas Show-o2 is an ≈ 1.5 \approx 1.5 B shared-Qwen flow model over 3D causal-VAE latents. These bases have complementary roles: Scale-RAE supports the full semantic/denoising × \times shared/frozen decomposition, whereas Show-o2 tests whether the aggregate failure and its diagnosis-guided repair recur under a different unified architecture. The architectural requirements also separate the transferable parts of the method. In a unified autoregressive generator with a shared self-verifier, capture, locking the reward read, and the complete drift-triggered anchor controller—including its trigger statistic, TopK selection, and residual propagation—remain well-defined because they operate on rollout-level scalar reads rather than continuous flow states. The dense latent component used here specifically exploits continuous generation latents by re-noising each terminal sample at prescribed noise levels. For autoregressive generators, process-dense supervision could instead operate over prefixes; for masked-token or discrete-diffusion generators, its natural counterpart is scoring partially masked states at multiple mask ratios. Removing the intermediate noise levels, 𝒯 = { 0 } \mathcal{T}=\{0\} , recovers the terminal self-reward used by the measured terminal-anchor arm. At q = 1 / 16 q=1/16 , this arm remains jointly non-inferior to the every-rollout grounding steelman on both bases (Appendix G.2 ). Dense scoring therefore lifts an already viable locked-and-anchored construction rather than making the construction viable. Shared trainable weights mark the structural boundary of rewriting. With a genuinely separate fixed judge, the problem reduces to the static-proxy setting, where exploitation and staleness remain the relevant failure modes.

sections.heading: G.3 Structural Ladder, Anchor-Dose, and KL Sweep
sections.text: This subsection reports the repair-validation study. On training-internal instruments it establishes three facts: (i) severing the trainable coupling of the verifier removes the judge-rewriting route but leaves a standalone exploitation residual; (ii) sparse external anchors remove that residual as coverage increases; and (iii) a proximity (KL) penalty cannot achieve the same separation at any strength. All readouts here are the diagnostic instruments defined in Appendix B —the shared–frozen divergence gap (which identifies judge rewriting), the fixed-probe AUC loss, and the external-panel change (a panel- z z margin, where more negative is worse)— measured over 2,000 2{,}000 training steps on five seeds. These are internal-instrument units, not GenEval or DPG points. The ladder is a separately run structural-intervention study, distinct from the diagnostic factorial in Appendix E . One tolerance governs every external-panel readout below: δ panel = 0.17 \delta_{\mathrm{panel}}=0.17 , the one-sided external-retention tolerance obtained as the 95 % 95\% half-width of the θ 0 \theta_{0} -null distribution of the external-panel change. Retention requires a change ≥ − δ panel \geq-\delta_{\mathrm{panel}} ; positive changes remain inside the retained region. Thus “the residual persists” means a change more negative than − 0.17 -0.17 .

sections.heading: Wall-clock.
sections.text: Two all-external references bound the cost of the anchored arms. Scoring every rollout with the external panel costs 7.43 7.43 s/step; the grounding steelman, which additionally runs a VLM over every decoded image, costs 10.38 10.38 s/step. Against these, terminal anchoring at q = 1 / 16 q=1/16 runs at 2.64 2.64 s/step ( 2.8 × 2.8\times faster than the panel), and adding dense latent scoring at the same coverage costs almost nothing extra— 2.88 2.88 s/step for fixed-dose and 2.91 2.91 s/step for the controller, still a 2.6 × 2.6\times advantage over the panel and 3.6 × 3.6\times over the steelman that both of them outperform on the official benchmarks. sections.heading: H.3 Sampler and Solver
sections.text: Final evaluation and rollout sampling use a 50 50 -step Euler solver on the flow ODE. Rollout exploration draws independent initial noises x T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) from the current policy and transports them with the policy velocity field. Scale-RAE uses guidance level 1.0 1.0 , and Show-o2 uses guidance scale 5.0 5.0 ; each setting is fixed across all arms of its base. The sampler, resolution, and numerical precision are also held fixed within each base.

sections.heading: Training pool.
sections.text: Training prompts come from the MS-COCO train2017 captions. We sort caption annotations by annotation ID and retain the first caption for each of the 118,287 118{,}287 image IDs, giving one deterministic prompt per image without reweighting a scene through its five paraphrases. We apply Unicode NFKC normalization, lowercase the text, replace punctuation with spaces, collapse consecutive whitespace, and strip leading and trailing whitespace. Removing normalized duplicates leaves 117,574 117{,}574 unique captions.

sections.heading: Benchmark decontamination.
sections.text: The normalized pool contains no exact match to either evaluation benchmark. To remove near-verbatim overlap, for a training caption a a and benchmark prompt b b we compute C ⁡ ( a , b ) = LCS token ⁡ ( a , b ) min ⁡ { | a | , | b | } , C(a,b)=\frac{\operatorname{LCS}_{\mathrm{token}}(a,b)}{\min\{|a|,|b|\}}, where LCS token \operatorname{LCS}_{\mathrm{token}} is token-level longest common subsequence length. If both strings contain at least five normalized tokens, we remove a a whenever C ⁡ ( a , b ) ≥ 0.80 C(a,b)\geq 0.80 . This removes 186 186 captions matched to GenEval and 5 5 matched to DPG-Bench; the two sets are disjoint. The resulting frozen pool contains 117,383 117{,}383 prompts and no exact or near-verbatim benchmark match. Thus decontamination removes only 0.16 % 0.16\% of the normalized pool rather than reshaping its prompt distribution. sections.heading: Per-run streams.
sections.text: Each optimizer step uses one prompt group with G = 12 G=12 candidate rollouts. For each training seed, we deterministically shuffle the frozen pool and take the first 2,000 2{,}000 prompts without replacement. Every run therefore sees exactly 2,000 2{,}000 distinct prompts, with no repeated draw. All arms sharing a seed use the same prompts in the same order; different seeds use their own deterministic permutations. Both bases use this frozen pool and per-seed stream construction.

sections.heading: Evaluation isolation.
sections.text: Two official benchmarks are used for held-out utility, each with four images per prompt: GenEval ( 553 553 prompts, reported on a 0 0 – 1 1 scale) and DPG-Bench ( 1,065 1{,}065 prompts, reported on a 0 0 – 100 100 scale). Their prompt strings are consulted before training only by the exclusion rule above; they are never model inputs or reward inputs. Benchmark scorers and scores are used only for final evaluation of the fixed step- 2,000 2{,}000 checkpoint, never to construct rewards, select training prompts, tune hyperparameters, or choose checkpoints. GenEval additionally supplies the prespecified exploitation gate. The pretrained checkpoint θ 0 \theta_{0} is evaluated with the same sampler and benchmark implementation as the trained arms. Sampler, guidance, resolution, precision, prompt sets, and evaluation code are fixed across arms.

sections.heading: H.5 External Scorers and Aggregation
sections.text: The external supervision and comparator models are frozen and parameter-disjoint, and the held-out evaluators remain separate from the reward read under study: • Sparse training anchors and continuous diagnostic panel : HPSv2, PickScore, and ImageReward. Each scorer is standardized once on frozen θ 0 \theta_{0} generations and the standardized scores are averaged. This puts the scorers on a common scale and zero-centers the reference distribution; the frozen scorers and fixed normalizers keep the panel stationary throughout training. The same panel serves as the continuous diagnostic external signal. • Official evaluation : GenEval and DPG-Bench. • External-panel all-external control : the same external panel applied to every decoded rollout ( q = 1 q{=}1 ). • Grounding steelman : a frozen, parameter-disjoint Qwen2.5-VL-7B that reads the decoded image and answers the same prompt-alignment question as the latent semantic verifier, applied to every decoded rollout ( q = 1 q{=}1 ). Because it matches the construct that GenEval and DPG-Bench measure, it is a strong construct-matched all-external configuration and the primary active comparator of Appendix D . The frozen-reference standardization is what makes the external panel a stable target across checkpoints; the panel is never adapted to the policy.

sections.heading: H.6 Seed and Bootstrap Units
sections.text: Every reported utility arm is trained with five seeds, and arm-to-arm contrasts use the training seed as the replication unit with prompts paired within each seed. The pretrained checkpoint θ 0 \theta_{0} has no training-seed replication. Its prompt-bootstrap SE enters the margin floor, while learned-arm comparisons against it use paired hierarchical-bootstrap intervals over seeds and prompts. These are the units only; the confidence-interval construction, the non-inferiority margin rule, the joint decision, and the exact non-parametric tests that operate on them are defined in Appendix D and are not restated here.

sections.heading: H.7 Hardware and Software
sections.text: Experiments run on a single Ubuntu 20.04 node with 8 × 8\times NVIDIA L20 GPUs, each with 48 48 GiB of device memory. The host CPU model is AMD EPYC 7763, and the node has 512 512 GiB of system memory. The devices run independent seeds and arms in parallel. The software environment uses Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.2.0 with CUDA 12.1 and cuDNN 8.9.2, torchvision 0.17.0, Transformers 4.37.0, Diffusers 0.27.2, Accelerate 0.23.0, and PEFT 0.4.0. sections.heading: Appendix I Human Evaluation
sections.text: This appendix reports a blind, paired human rating study on representative Scale-RAE outputs. It provides direct human evidence that the prompt-faithfulness loss accompanying unanchored closed-loop self-reward is visible, characterizes that deviation, and measures how closely the automated instruments used elsewhere in this supplement track human judgment. The statistical rules are fixed in Appendix D.7 ; arm definitions and their automated scores are in Appendix G , and the checkpoint, sampler, prompt sets, and external-panel composition are in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Items.
sections.text: The study uses 100 100 prompts drawn by a fixed random sample from the two official benchmarks: 50 50 from GenEval, stratified over its categories, and 50 50 from DPG-Bench. Each prompt yields one image per arm, generated at the step- 2,000 2{,}000 checkpoint of the seed whose GenEval score is the median over the five training seeds. The initial noise is shared across arms, so the two images of a pair differ only in the arm that produced them.

sections.heading: Blocks.
sections.text: Three paired blocks are rated, each on all 100 100 prompts: • P1 : the pretrained checkpoint θ 0 \theta_{0} against the frozen-semantic diagnostic endpoint; • P2 : θ 0 \theta_{0} against the shared-semantic diagnostic endpoint; • P3 : the dense controller at q = 1 / 16 q{=}1/16 against the grounding steelman at q = 1 q{=}1 . P1 and P2 are the two unanchored semantic cells of Appendix E ; P3 is the primary active comparator against the full method of Appendix F .

sections.heading: Questions.
sections.text: Every item asks Q1 and Q2, each with an explicit “cannot tell” option. Q1, the primary question, asks which image better matches the prompt; Q2 asks which image is better rendered, independently of the prompt. Items in P1 and P2 carry two further questions. Q3a is a multi-select failure-mode tag over object category, count, color or attribute, spatial relation, action or pose, scene or context, and cannot articulate , shown only after a rater judges the post-RL image less faithful in Q1. Q3b is a single-select question, asked on every P1 and P2 item, asking which image, if either, shows visible distortion or artifacts.

sections.heading: Annotators and blinding.
sections.text: Four non-author annotators with no prior involvement in the work were recruited, and three were retained after the catch-trial screen below. All were non-experts in generative modeling. Annotators received only the rating instructions and were informed of neither the research question, the systems’ identities, nor which arm produced which image. Within every item the two images were shown in randomized left–right order, and item order was shuffled independently per annotator. Participation was voluntary, annotators were told that their ratings would be used in a research publication, and no personal data were collected.

sections.text: Each block carries 10 10 catch items in which one candidate image is generated from an unrelated prompt, giving 30 30 catch judgments per annotator. One of the four annotators fell below the prespecified 0.800 0.800 retention threshold and was excluded in full before analysis. The three retained annotators pass 87 87 of 90 90 catch judgments ( 0.967 0.967 ) and contribute three judgments per item, or 300 300 per block.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.16500v1 [cs.CV] 12 Oct 2026 Self-Verifier Capture in Unified Visual Generators: Diagnosing and Repairing Closed-Loop Self-Reward Binyan Chen Tong Pan Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Email: sztn@mail.ustc.edu.cn pantong@mail.ustc.edu.cn Abstract Image-space reward requires decoding and a separate judge; unified visual generators can instead reuse their understanding pathway for decode-free, self-supplied reward. Optimizing against this verifier closes the self-reward loop; shared trainable weights let one update move generation and scoring even with the reward gradient stopped. We call the resulting failure self-verifier capture : self-reward rises while independently measured quality falls. Matched semantic/denoising × \times shared/frozen cells on Scale-RAE isolate two routes: the policy exploits on-manifold blind spots of a frozen semantic judge, while shared updates additionally rewrite the judge. A frozen judge also becomes stale, and repeated self-refresh yields progressively weaker recoveries. The diagnosis yields a two-part repair: locking the warmed reward read blocks rewriting, while sparse, parameter-disjoint external anchors counter residual exploitation. Unanchored rollouts retain semantic reward across multiple latent noise levels—dense latent reward that terminal image-space judging cannot supply—while a drift-triggered controller allocates anchors to high-drift rollouts and propagates their calibration within each group. At matched budgets, the controller improves on fixed-dose anchoring, increasingly so as coverage tightens. Both the unanchored failure and the repair transfer to the higher-performing, architecturally distinct Show-o2. Across both bases, the complete method significantly outperforms a construct-matched every-rollout judge on GenEval and DPG-Bench while externally scoring only 1 / 16 1/16 of rollouts. At 1 / 32 1/32 coverage, it scores higher in all four comparisons and remains jointly non-inferior. 1 Introduction Unified visual generators increasingly place understanding and generation in a shared model and latent space ( Xie et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025b ; Tong et al., 2026 ) . Their understanding pathway can supply decode-free self-reward without rendering pixels or training a separate judge. Yet the same trainable sharing couples policy and judge: optimization can change both the generated samples and the function that scores them. Learned proxies are known to become unreliable when optimized beyond their fitting regime ( Gao et al., 2023 ) , but the usual proxy-overoptimization picture treats the judge as fixed. A unified generator instead closes the reward loop. We call its characteristic failure self-verifier capture : optimization raises self-reward while independently measured quality falls. Capture may arise by exploiting a fixed judge’s blind spots or by rewriting a shared judge. Distinguishing these routes matters because the natural defense—a frozen reward read—severs only the parameter path: as Fig. 1 shows, it blocks rewriting but leaves distributional search against a static verifier. Figure 1: Two routes through closed-loop self-reward. A policy update can search a fixed verifier’s blind spots (blue, exploiting ); with trainable weight sharing, the same update can also move the verifier (orange, rewriting ). We separate them on Scale-RAE with a matched 2 × 2 2\times 2 design crossing semantic versus denoising verifiers with shared versus frozen reward reads. The comparison reveals that a frozen semantic verifier remains exploitable on-manifold, shared updates additionally rewrite its scoring function, and the isolated verifier grows stale, while the capacity-matched denoising control shows no such capture. The aggregate failure recurs on the higher-performing, architecturally distinct Show-o2, despite its VQA-trained understanding pathway and semantic distillation on noisy latents. The diagnosis directly specifies the repair. A stop-gradient on the advantage blocks only the direct path, so we lock the warmed reward read against indirect shared-weight rewriting, then use sparse, parameter-disjoint external anchors to calibrate and gate rollouts while retaining dense latent self-reward. A drift-triggered controller places the limited anchors. Evaluation against construct-matched every-rollout external judges shows that dense latent reward and selective anchoring substantially improve both utility and external-decode efficiency across bases. Our contributions are: • We formulate unified visual self-reward as a closed-loop judge problem and show that aggregate capture recurs across two architectures. • A matched shared–frozen study separates static exploitation from shared-judge rewriting and measures subsequent staleness. • We derive a diagnosis-guided repair combining structural isolation, independent anchors, dense latent reward, and adaptive allocation. • At 16 × 16\times lower external-decode coverage, the complete method significantly outperforms a construct-matched every-rollout judge on both benchmarks and bases; at 32 × 32\times , it scores higher in all four comparisons while remaining jointly non-inferior. 2 Related Work Proxy overoptimization and self-judging loops. Optimizing a learned reward beyond its fitting regime raises the proxy while degrading the intended objective ( Gao et al., 2023 ) . Self-rewarding language models turn model-generated evaluations into training signals within the broader LLM-as-a-judge paradigm, where evaluators can favor their own outputs ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . In text-domain reasoning, this loop induces a confidence-conditioned coupling between a policy’s rollouts and its intrinsic rewards ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , and reward-model mismatch under policy shift already motivates iterated RLHF, which refreshes preferences on current-policy outputs ( Wolf et al., 2025 ) . Classical reward tampering provides a related coordinate but frames the failure as an agent corrupting a separate reward channel ( Everitt et al., 2021 ) . These lines establish self-favoring bias, statistical policy–reward coupling, distribution shift, and separate-channel failure, yet do not isolate a scoring function that moves through shared policy–judge parameters—the route a unified generator opens. Intrinsic and latent rewards for visual generation. Several visual post-training methods avoid an external image reward, deriving intrinsic signals from the generator itself—self-certainty for autoregressive text-to-image optimization ( Chen et al., 2025 ) or frozen-decoder pixel reconstruction ( Liao et al., 2025 ) . SOLACE instead turns an online denoiser’s noise-recovery confidence into reward ( Kim and Cho, 2026 ) . These signals measure token uncertainty, reconstruction fidelity, or denoising confidence rather than free-running semantic judgment through a unified understanding pathway; SOLACE therefore motivates our denoising-verifier control. Closer to our setting, a complementary line freezes the understanding pathway: LatentUM reflects on generated content through a frozen evaluator ( Jin et al., 2026a ) , while SRUM caches a unified model’s internal evaluations offline and trains its flow by reward-weighted regression ( Jin et al., 2026b ) . These staged designs sidestep the online shared-weight loop, but do not test whether a frozen evaluator remains calibrated as the policy moves or compare frozen and shared reads to separate static exploitation from judge rewriting. On the optimization side, visual-generation RL spans diffusion-policy optimization and flow-native GRPO ( Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) ; KVPO introduces the TVE–Gibbs policy surrogate for ODE-native preference optimization in autoregressive video generation ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . External rewards. Frozen, prompt-conditioned image-space models such as ImageReward, HPSv2, and PickScore provide parameter-independent preference signals over decoded images, spanning prompt alignment and perceptual quality ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Kirstain et al., 2023 ) . However, they operate only after decoding and score the terminal image, making every-rollout evaluation costly and providing neither decode-free nor dense latent reward. Together, prior work leaves open how to diagnose and repair a trainable semantic judge inside the generator without surrendering dense, decode-free reward. 3 Diagnosing Self-Verifier Capture A rising self-score paired with falling external quality establishes a failure, but does not reveal its source. Matched Scale-RAE comparisons reveal self-verifier capture through both exploitation of a frozen judge and rewriting of a shared one; a frozen reward read also becomes stale, and the failure recurs on the stronger, architecturally distinct Show-o2. Our diagnosis-guided repair locks the warmed reward read, preserves dense latent reward, and allocates sparse, parameter-disjoint external anchors with a drift-triggered controller. Across both bases, it significantly outperforms a construct-matched every-rollout judge on both benchmarks at 16 × 16\times lower decode coverage; at 32 × 32\times , joint non-inferiority still holds with all four point estimates higher.
